name: Basilar (pontine) territory
summary: The basilar territory is the pons and the ventral midbrain supplied by the paramedian, short circumferential and long circumferential branches of the basilar artery. This level-1 domain covers the whole pons, so it includes the paramedian pontine lacunes of small vessel disease (pure motor hemiparesis, ataxic hemiparesis, dysarthria-clumsy hand), the lateral pontine syndromes of the circumferential branches (Millard-Gubler, Foville and the AICA syndrome), and the bilateral ventral pontine infarction of basilar occlusion that produces the locked-in state. The paramedian branches are end-arteries with no collateral, which is why the pons is the commonest brainstem site of lacunes and of hypertensive hemorrhage.

anatomy.location: The entire pons (basis and tegmentum) and the ventral and paramedian midbrain, from the pontomedullary junction to the interpeduncular fossa, including the middle cerebellar peduncle's proximal part; paramedian branches supply the medial basis and tegmentum, short circumferential branches the lateral basis, and long circumferential branches (AICA, SCA) the lateral tegmentum and peduncles; bounded below by the vertebral and PICA territories of the medulla and above by the PCA thalamic and midbrain domains.

afferents.from: Paramedian, short circumferential and long circumferential branches of the basilar artery

efferents.to: Anterior pontomesencephalic vein and petrosal veins

function: The territory contains the corticospinal and corticopontine fibers of the basis pontis, the pontine nuclei, the medial lemniscus and MLF, the abducens and facial nuclei and the pontine gaze center, the trigeminal nuclei, the vestibular and cochlear nuclei, the locus coeruleus and the pontine reticular formation that sustains consciousness and breathing, so ischemia produces the crossed pontine syndromes (ipsilateral VI or VII palsy with contralateral hemiparesis), internuclear ophthalmoplegia and gaze palsy, and, when bilateral, coma or the locked-in state. Thrombosis of the basilar trunk, embolism to its top and hypertensive lipohyalinosis of its perforators are the three mechanisms.

bestView.label: pontine domain of the basilar perforators

imaging.normalAppearance: On the overlay the basilar domain covers the pons and ventral midbrain; on imaging a paramedian pontine infarct is a wedge of restricted diffusion reaching the ventral surface and stopping at the midline.

pathology.finding: Unilateral wedge of restricted diffusion in the basis pontis reaching the ventral surface with pure motor or ataxic hemiparesis; early DWI may be negative.

pathology.pathology: Basilar occlusion with bilateral pontine infarction
pathology.finding: Bilateral ventral pontine restricted diffusion with locked-in syndrome or coma; hyperdense basilar on CT and absent flow on CTA.
Central pontine hyperdensity with coma, pinpoint reactive pupils, quadriplegia and ocular bobbing; large hemorrhages are fatal.

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral hemiparesis with ipsilateral VI or VII palsy
lesionEffects.mechanism: Paramedian and lateral pontine infarction (crossed syndromes)

lesionEffects.deficit: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia and horizontal gaze palsy
lesionEffects.mechanism: MLF and pontine gaze center infarction
Bilateral basis pontis infarction sparing the tegmentum

examination: Horizontal eye movements, facial strength and corneal reflexes
Strength and coordination on the side opposite the cranial nerve signs
Consciousness, pupils and breathing in bilateral disease
pearls: Pontine lacunes mimic capsular lacunes; the eyes and the face give them away
Locked-in patients are awake: ask them to blink or look up before you decide they are comatose
The basilar perforators have no collaterals and no forgiveness
